vectors.note: Rules run after whitespace is collapsed, so a two-word `from` matches across any whitespace.
`to` is inserted as text: `$$` is two dollar signs, not a replacement pattern.
`$&` inserts a dollar sign, a symbol, and an ampersand, which is punctuation and removed like any other.
Rules apply in listed order, each to the output of the one before: a -> b -> c.
The same rules in the other order: a -> b, and the rule before it never sees the result.
One edit from each candidate: the transcript wins the tie, so candidateIndex is 0.
The emoji is one code point (two UTF-16 units): 11 characters, two of them missing (the space before the emoji, and the emoji).
A lone surrogate is read as U+FFFD, the replacement character: one character, never rejected.
Locale-insensitive toLowerCase, as the reference implementation: the dotted capital I lowercases to i plus a combining dot, one edit.
Reachable on stale data only (the schema refuses the transcript): no candidate survives, so the score is 0 and there are no details.
candidateIndex is the ORIGINAL position: 1 names acceptedTranscripts[0].
Exactly the cap is not over it: the boundary of the truncation, pinned.
A rule the schema would refuse (stale data) is skipped, never thrown on: the exam scorer must not crash on a stored row.

Two hundred emoji are 200 code points and 400 UTF-16 units: at the cap, so the rule applies.
The boundary before a one-letter rule is required too: "a" inside "ba" is not a word.
A combining mark belongs to its word: the rule for "eight" leaves "all eight" alone.
The first rule inserts its words only, so the second finds no "!" to rewrite: punctuation in a rewrite is ignored, as it is in the comparison.
A rewrite that normalises to nothing would delete a word; the schema refuses it, and the scorer skips it in stale data.
Lowercasing J + COMBINING CARON exposes a pair NFC composes; the rules read the composed letter.

A boundary is required only at an edge of the rule that is a letter, mark or digit, so "&" fires where it touches letters; its rewrite is set apart from them by spaces, so rock&roll reads as rock and roll.

Japanese is written without spaces, so a rewrite that starts in Katakana is not set apart from the digit before it.
